studies.title: Limits Drawn Around A Parting
studies.meaning: The surah opens on the hardest moment in a marriage and immediately slows it down. A waiting period is set and the parties are told to count it, which turns an act that could be finished in a sentence into a process with a duration. Then a striking provision: the woman stays in the home she was living in, and is not to be put out. The ayah closes with a clause that has no legal force at all and is the reason for everything before it. You do not know; God may bring something new about after this.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. Before this surah, separation in Arabia could be instant and the woman's position afterwards depended entirely on her family's willingness to take her back. Sending her out of the house was normal. The commentators connect the surah broadly to a case brought to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) in which a separation had been declared carelessly, though the reports differ; what they agree on is that the surah introduced a delay where there had been none.

keyTerms.note: From the root for counting. The word names a measured interval rather than a rule, and its presence turns the whole passage into a matter of elapsed time, which is what gives anything else a chance to happen.

The word for the edge of a field or the border of a territory, not for a punishment. It pictures an enclosed space with room inside it, which is how the classical commentators read the phrase wherever it appears.
A verb for causing something to come into being that was not there before. Used of God at the end of this ayah, it leaves the future genuinely open rather than merely unknown to the parties.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A household in Medina was a compound of rooms around a shared yard, and a woman leaving it went back to her father or brother if she had one and to nothing much if she did not. There were no separate dwellings to move into and no income she could carry with her. The instruction that she stays where she is, in the middle of a quarrel, was therefore a material provision before it was anything else.
studies.didYouKnow: The surah is addressed in its first words to the Prophet in the singular and then switches immediately to the plural for the instruction itself. Classical grammarians note the shift and read it as addressing the community through him. The same opening pattern occurs in a handful of other places, usually where the subject is something the whole community will have to practise.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage treats an ending as something that might not be one. Every provision in it works against finality: a counted interval, a shared roof, a warning against pushing anyone out, and then an explicit statement that God may produce a situation nobody can currently see. That last clause is the theological heart. It says the future is not a projection of the present, which is a claim about God's action rather than about the couple's feelings.

crossReferences.why: Says you may dislike something in which God has placed a great deal of good, speaking of marriage.
Sets out the waiting period at greater length and names reconciliation as the purpose of the interval.
Describes arbitrators appointed from both families, with reconciliation as the stated aim.

studies.applyIt: The next time you decide something in anger, write the decision down and do nothing for three days. Not because you will change your mind. Because this ayah puts a counted interval in the one place people most want speed, and then says you do not know what might arrive in it. Find out whether that is true in something small.

studies.title: A Way Out And Unreckoned Provision
studies.meaning: The order is even on both sides, and that is the point. Keep them well or part from them well. The same word for decency is used twice, so a parting is asked to be handled with the care of a repair. Witnesses are called, and they are told to testify for God, not for either side. Then the passage lifts clear of its subject. Mindfulness of God is promised an opening, and supply from a direction nobody counted on.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in a short surah given over to the ending of marriages. Some reports tie the opening of the surah to one case in Medina, though the accounts differ over who was involved. The setting is clear enough. A woman leaving a marriage had no standing of her own. The details of timing, housing and upkeep decided whether she ended up with nothing.

keyTerms.note: From the root for knowing. It names what a community knows to be right without listing it, so the standard is what any decent person would recognise as fair treatment.
A noun of place from the verb to go out. It names a door rather than a rescue, so what is promised is an opening in a situation rather than the removal of the situation.
From the root for counting and keeping accounts. The supply comes from a column the person had not entered in his own ledger, which is an exact way of saying unforeseen rather than miraculous.
From the same counting root as the phrase above, so the two lines are linked by sound. What is enough for a person is named with the words of arithmetic rather than of feeling.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A divorced woman in seventh-century Arabia went back to her father or her brothers. If they were dead or unwilling, she had nothing. There was no paid work for women, and in most cases no property she could hold alone. The call for witnesses put a private decision in front of two men who would remember it. That was the only record such a community could keep.
studies.didYouKnow: The promise in these two ayat is quoted far more often than the subject it belongs to. An early companion is reported to have said that if people would only take hold of this one ayah, it would be enough for them. The placing is deliberate. The widest promise in the surah arrives in the middle of rules about a marriage ending.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Putting a broad promise inside a passage about parting says something about where God is expected to act. Not only in prayer or in crisis. Also in the arrangements people make when a bond has failed, which is where behaviour is worst and least watched. The promise itself is worded with care: a way out and supply nobody counted on, not a reversal. And enough is offered to the one who hands the outcome over.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same paired instruction in the longest surah, keeping or parting, with the same standard on both.
Shows provision arriving from an unreckoned direction as a scene rather than a promise.
Puts the same word for sufficiency in the mouths of people under threat, as a reply rather than a promise.

studies.applyIt: Think of a relationship that ended badly, at work or in your family. Then ask one question: did you end it in a way you would be willing to have described out loud. If not, there is usually one thing still open, a message unsent or an amount unreturned. The passage asks for decency at the exit, which is the part nobody watches.
studies.explainEasier: When a marriage ends, God says to keep the person kindly or let them go kindly. Two fair people should watch. He also promises that anyone who is careful with him will find a way out, and help he did not expect.

studies.title: Terms Counted In Months
studies.meaning: The ayah extends the interval to cases the earlier passage did not cover, and its tone is administrative rather than moral. Three situations are named and each is given a measure, with the last defined by an event rather than by a number: for a pregnancy, the term runs until the birth. Commentators note the care taken to leave no case unaddressed, since an uncounted interval would leave a woman without a defined position. The closing clause lifts the whole passage: awareness of God is met with ease in your affair.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The commentators record that the earlier passage on waiting periods left questions people then brought forward, and this ayah answers them. The reports differ over who asked. What is not in dispute is the effect: the ambiguity that had left certain women in an undefined state was closed, which in a society without courts of record mattered more than it might now.

keyTerms.note: The ordinary verb for giving up hope, used here of a bodily stage rather than of an emotion. Arabic names the phase by what a woman no longer expects, which is a gentler construction than a clinical term.

A verb for uncertainty that unsettles, stronger than simply not knowing. Its presence concedes that the people applying this passage may genuinely not know the answer, and provides for that rather than assuming expertise.
A noun for what is easy or unobstructed, the opposite of the word for hardship. Placed at the end of a legal passage, it promises smoothness in the handling rather than exemption from the situation.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Time in that world was kept by the moon and by the body. A month was a visible thing, from one crescent to the next, and dates for debts, pilgrimages and markets were fixed by it. Nobody carried a calendar; people counted. An interval measured in months was therefore something a whole household could observe together, and the counting itself was public in a way a private arrangement could never be.
studies.didYouKnow: Three of this surah's twelve ayat end with a promise attached to the same condition: whoever is mindful of God. The promises differ each time, a way out, ease in the matter, the covering of faults, and they are placed inside the legal material rather than gathered at the end. The chapter alternates instruction and consolation almost line by line.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah shows revelation attending to the least dramatic kind of difficulty. Nothing here is about belief or destiny; it is about whether a specific woman knows when a specific period ends. That the Quran spends an ayah on it says something about the scale at which divine attention is claimed to operate. And the closing promise attaches ease not to the outcome but to the conduct of the person handling it.

crossReferences.why: Gives the waiting period after a death, showing the same practice applied to a different kind of ending.
States that ease accompanies hardship, which is the promise this ayah attaches to mindfulness.
Describes the stages of pregnancy and birth as a sign, the event that closes the term named here.

studies.applyIt: Notice the next time you cannot bear not knowing how long something will last: an illness, a process, a wait for news. The discomfort is usually about the open end rather than the difficulty itself. Ask for a date if there is one to be had, and if there is not, write down what you will do each week regardless.

studies.title: Sent Down To You
studies.meaning: A short ayah that does two jobs. It closes the legal section by naming what has just been given as God's command, sent down, which places a set of practical arrangements in the same category as the rest of revelation. Then it attaches a promise that has nothing to do with the subject: for the one mindful of God, wrongs are covered over and reward enlarged. Commentators note that the promise is general and detachable, which is why this ayah is quoted far outside the context it sits in.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The surah's arrangement is worth noticing: instruction, then a promise, then more instruction, then this. The commentators report no occasion for the ayah itself. They treat it as the seal on the preceding passage, and note that the Quran regularly closes a section of practical material this way, by naming its source and adding something about the person who acts on it rather than about the act.

keyTerms.note: The standard verb for revelation, used here of practical arrangements about households. The Quran makes no distinction of vocabulary between the loftiest passages and the most domestic, which is itself a statement.
A verb meaning to make something great, applied to the reward rather than to the deed. The act stays the size it was; what changes is the valuation placed on it afterwards.
From a root meaning to shield or take precaution. It describes an attentive, protective posture rather than fear, and the surah repeats it as the single condition attached to every promise it makes.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Custom was the ordinary source of authority in Arabian domestic life. What a family did in a hard case was what its grandfathers had done, adjusted by whichever elder had standing that year, and disputes were settled by an appeal to precedent. To say that an arrangement had been sent down was to remove it from that machinery entirely, which was more startling in a household matter than in a theological one.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for command or affair occurs seven times in this short surah of twelve ayat, more often than in most chapters twice its length. It covers a human situation, a divine instruction, the conduct of a town and finally the command that descends through the heavens in the last ayah, so a single word threads the chapter from a household to the cosmos.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two things are established without argument. The first is that the domestic and the sacred are not separate categories: what has just been said about waiting periods and housing is called something sent down, in the same words used of the Quran itself. The second is a claim about proportion. A person who handles an ordinary difficulty with care is promised the covering of past faults, which treats conduct in a hard week as weighing more than its size suggests.

crossReferences.why: Attaches to the same mindfulness a criterion, the covering of wrongs, and forgiveness.
Promises the removal of bad deeds and reward according to the best of what was done.
States that avoiding the major wrongs brings the covering over of the lesser ones.

studies.applyIt: Take the least interesting obligation in your week: the form, the call, the thing you owe a relative. Do it properly rather than quickly, once. This ayah calls a set of household arrangements something sent down, which suggests the boring end of your life is not a lower category. Test that on one task and see whether the doing of it changes.

studies.title: Housed, Not Squeezed
studies.meaning: The ayah moves through a difficult period item by item, and what is striking is the motive it names. Housing is set at the level of the man's own means, and then pressure is ruled out in terms of intention: do not cause harm in order to make things narrow for them. Commentators read that clause as naming a specific tactic, discomfort applied until someone leaves on their own. Then payment for nursing, and an instruction to confer between yourselves in what is recognised as decent. Disagreement is anticipated and provided for without blame.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. A woman in this position had no independent household and often a nursing child, and the practical questions were immediate: where does she sleep, who feeds her, who pays for the milk. The commentators note that the ayah answers each in order. They report no single occasion, and read the passage as filling out what the surah's opening instruction about not putting anyone out of the house actually required day to day.

keyTerms.note: A noun from the verb to find, so it names what a person actually has available rather than a fixed standard. The provision scales to the household, which keeps the instruction possible for the poorest listener.

An intensive verb meaning to make a space narrow. Naming the purpose rather than the act is unusual, and it catches conduct that would look unobjectionable from outside while being designed to wear someone down.

A passive participle meaning what is known and acknowledged, so the standard is what decent people in a place would recognise as fair. The Quran uses it where a fixed rule would be too rigid for the situation.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Wet-nursing was an established trade in Arabia, with agreed rates and its own reputation network. Meccan families regularly sent infants to nurses among the desert tribes for their first years, believing the air and the language were better there. So a clause about paying a mother for nursing her own child was not strange economics. It named her work as work, in a market where everyone knew the going price.
studies.didYouKnow: The word the ayah uses for what the parties owe each other is the same word used across the Quran for ordinary decency, and it appears in more than thirty places. Classical jurists treated it as deliberately open, since what counts as recognised good conduct differs between a farming village and a trading town, and the Quran declined to fix it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage addresses itself to a motive, which is rare and revealing. It is possible to do nothing formally wrong and still make a person's life narrow enough that they leave, and the ayah names that possibility and closes it. What the Quran is protecting here is not a right but a person's dignity in a week when they have no leverage. The instruction to confer, rather than to command, points the same way.

crossReferences.why: Sets out nursing and its payment at greater length, with the same instruction to consult together.
Tells men to live with their wives in recognised good, using the same word this ayah uses.
Warns against retaining a spouse in order to cause harm, naming the same underlying motive.

studies.applyIt: Think of a situation where you have more leverage than the other person: a tenant, an employee, a family member who needs something from you. Ask yourself whether anything you are doing is designed to make them uncomfortable enough to give up. Stop that one thing this week. The ayah does not ask for generosity here. It asks you not to use pressure you have.

studies.title: Spend From What You Have
studies.meaning: Two orders, one for each kind of household. The wording takes care not to shame the second. The man of means spends from what he has room for. The man whose provision is measured out spends from what he was given. Then comes a general rule. God does not charge a soul beyond what He has handed it, so the demand is exactly the size of the means. The passage closes with a promise about order in time, not about amount.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in a surah about the ending of marriages and the upkeep owed afterwards. The ayah before it deals with housing and nursing, so this one speaks to men supporting a household they no longer live in. No set occasion is reported. Medina held households at both ends of the range this ayah describes, and both were listening.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning width and room. Wealth is described as having space rather than having much, so the instruction is to spend out of the room a person has.
A passive from the root for decree and measure. The narrower income is described as portioned out rather than as lacking, which lifts blame from the person in the same phrase that names his shortage.
A verb for laying a task on someone that costs them effort. The clause after it fixes the limit at what was given, so the measure is not human strength in general but this person's own holdings.
From a root meaning what is easy and, in older usage, the left hand, the side that does not strain. Both words in the closing promise are indefinite, so an ease is promised rather than the ease.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Income in Medina was seasonal and visible. A man's harvest was known to his neighbours to within a few sacks. There was no way to hide a bad year or to talk up a good one. That made a rule pegged to means workable, and also kind. Nobody could be accused of holding back beyond what the street already knew he had.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran states the relation between hardship and ease twice, in two different shapes. Here ease is promised after hardship, in sequence. In a short Meccan surah the wording is different: ease is said to be with hardship, alongside it rather than following it. Classical readers noticed the difference and kept both.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah fits the demand to the person rather than to a fixed bar. That changes what falling short means for someone poor. It also puts a floor under the poorer man. He is told to spend, not let off, so he keeps the dignity of giving along with the limit. The closing promise then meets the worry the order creates. It is worded as a sequence, which lets the hardship be real while it lasts.

crossReferences.why: Gives the other shape of the same promise, ease placed alongside hardship rather than after it.
States the same limit in the widest form, closing the longest surah with it.
Gives the same two-tier arrangement in the longest surah, using the same distinction between ample and restricted means.

studies.applyIt: If money is tight, give something small anyway this week. Give it without apology and without explaining. The ayah refuses to let a person off giving because they have little. It also refuses to measure them against anyone else. Both halves matter, and most people only apply one of them to themselves.
studies.explainEasier: God says that a rich person should give from what he has, and a person with little should give from the little he has. God never asks anyone for more than he gave them. He promises that ease comes after hard times.

studies.title: Towns That Were Reckoned With
studies.meaning: The surah turns without warning from household arrangements to the fate of whole settlements, and the commentators read the juxtaposition as the argument. The same word is used for the divine command that the town defied and for the instruction just given about a marriage. Then a sequence: strict accounting, then punishment, then a taste of the consequence, then a final outcome named as loss. The word for their affair appears three times in two ayat, so what they did and what became of it are described with one noun.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The surah has spent seven ayat on domestic conduct and now invokes vanished peoples, which reads as abrupt until the vocabulary is noticed. The commentators do not attach an occasion to the pair. They point out that the Quran often closes a passage of practical instruction by widening the frame, so that behaviour inside a household is set against the same standard applied to whole communities.

keyTerms.note: A verb for going beyond a limit with insolence, used of a river bursting its banks and of an animal that will not be handled. It describes defiance as excess rather than as opposition.

keyTerms.gloss: so We called it to account
keyTerms.note: The verb for settling an account between two parties, from the root for counting. Applied to a town it treats the outcome as a reckoning of what was already on the books rather than as an arbitrary blow.

A commercial word for the shortfall left when a venture closes below its cost. Ending the account with it keeps the whole passage inside the language of bookkeeping that the surah before it also draws on.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A town in that world was a settlement with water, walls of a kind, and a market: small enough that everyone knew who held the wells and how the disputes had gone. When one failed, it failed completely, and the ruins stayed visible for centuries on routes people still used. Arabians did not learn about vanished communities from books. They camped beside them and told the stories at the fire.
studies.didYouKnow: The first of these two ayat uses the verb for calling to account and then the noun from the same root immediately after it, a construction Arabic uses for emphasis: the verb followed by its own noun. The same doubling occurs with the word for punishment in the same line, so the passage stacks two of these intensifying pairs back to back.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage refuses a distinction most people make without noticing. What a town does to its messengers and what a household does in a hard month are named with the same word for command, so obedience is not a public category with a private exemption. The accounting language then makes a further point: the outcome described is arithmetic rather than temper. A record was kept, and the total was read out.

crossReferences.why: Names towns destroyed with the strike arriving at night or during the midday rest.
Counts how many towns were destroyed while doing wrong, leaving wells abandoned and palaces empty.
Describes the sequence by which a town's affluent overstep and the word then falls due upon it.

studies.applyIt: Pick one commitment you keep in public and break in private: punctuality, tone, honesty about small numbers. Name it out loud to yourself this week, without resolving to fix it yet. The passage sets a household and a city under one word, which suggests the two versions of you are being read as one record rather than two.

studies.title: You Who Have Kernels
studies.meaning: The address is unusual and worth pausing on. Believers are called by a phrase that means those who possess the inner substance of a thing, which classical commentators gloss as sound understanding. The appeal is therefore to intelligence rather than to obedience, in a surah that has just been giving practical instructions. What follows is a statement, not a command: God has sent down to you a reminder. The word for reminder is then identified in the next ayah, in a way that surprises most readers.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The ayah sits between the account of destroyed towns and the description of the messenger, and the commentators read it as the hinge. They report no occasion. What they note is the composition of the address: the phrase about understanding is joined to the phrase about believing, so the audience is defined by both at once rather than by either alone, which is not the Quran's usual practice.

keyTerms.note: The plural of the word for the kernel inside a shell or the heart of a date stone. Arabic names the understanding by the edible part, so intelligence is pictured as what remains when the husk is removed.

A word covering both the act of recalling and the thing that prompts it. Left indefinite here, it is identified in the next ayah, and that identification is the surprise the passage is building toward.

The surah's recurring verb, here in the imperative and addressed to people already described as believing. Mindfulness is presented as something believers are still being asked for, not as a state they have reached.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Dates were the staple of Medina and everyone handled them constantly, splitting the fruit from its stone, storing the flesh, feeding the rest to animals. The vocabulary of shell and kernel came from that daily sorting. Calling someone a person of kernels was not an abstract compliment. It meant they had got past the outside of a thing, the way you do a hundred times before noon when the harvest is in.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase translated as people of understanding occurs sixteen times in the Quran, and almost every occurrence follows a sign or a piece of evidence rather than a command. The Book calls on that faculty when it wants something weighed, which makes its appearance here, straight after an account of ruined towns, consistent with the pattern.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah makes understanding part of the religious address rather than an alternative to it. Believers are named by their reasoning and asked to be careful in the same breath, which treats those two as working together rather than as rivals. And the reminder is described as sent down, which places the object of thought outside the thinker. The faculty is honoured; it is not asked to generate the content on its own.

crossReferences.why: Addresses the same people of understanding, after the heavens and the alternation of night and day.
Asks whether those who know and those who do not are equal, and answers by naming the same group.
Describes a blessed Book sent down so that people of understanding may reflect on its signs.

studies.applyIt: Take one belief you hold because you inherited it and spend twenty minutes this week finding out why it is held. Not to overturn it. To move it from the shell to the kernel. The ayah addresses believers by their capacity to think and then hands them something to think about, which is a different relationship from being told.

studies.title: A Reminder Who Is A Person
studies.meaning: The previous ayah said a reminder had been sent down, and this one identifies it: a messenger. Commentators read the grammar in two ways, either as the messenger being the reminder himself or as him accompanying it, and both readings are preserved. What follows is the purpose, stated as movement: to bring people out of darknesses into the light. The plural on the first and the singular on the second is consistent across the Quran. Darkness is many; light is one.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, and the surah is closing. Having spent most of its length on a difficult private situation, it ends by describing what the whole revelation is for. The commentators report no occasion for the ayah. They note the shape of the surah instead: it opens on a household, widens to ruined cities, and closes on the heavens, with this ayah as the step that moves from history to the reader's own condition.

keyTerms.note: An active participle: the signs do the clarifying rather than merely being clear themselves. The form makes them an instrument, something that shows other things, which fits the movement out of darkness described next.

A plural, always, wherever the Quran pairs it with light. The commentators read the number as meaning that there are many ways of not seeing and only one of seeing, which the grammar states without argument.

The surah's recurring root for what is given, used earlier of provision arriving from an unexpected direction and here of what waits in the garden. Ending with it ties the two halves of the chapter together in a single word.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Night in the desert is not dim; it is absolute, and then extraordinarily bright when the moon is up. Travellers moved at night in summer and read the ground by starlight, and a single lamp in a doorway could be seen across a whole settlement. The difference between having light and not having it was total rather than gradual, which is why the image works without needing to be explained.
studies.didYouKnow: The pairing of darkness and light occurs in the Quran more than a dozen times, and in every one of them darkness is plural and light is singular. The consistency is complete enough that the grammarians treat it as a deliberate feature of the Book's usage rather than a stylistic habit.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Calling a person a reminder is the striking move. Revelation is not only a text to be consulted but a life that was lived where people could watch it, which is why the tradition preserved the messenger's conduct alongside the words. The ayah also describes guidance as extraction rather than instruction: someone is brought out, which implies they could not simply walk. That is a modest and honest account of how people change.

crossReferences.why: Says God brings the believers out of darknesses into the light, using the same verb and pairing.
States that the Book was sent down so the messenger might bring people out of darknesses into light.
Names the messenger himself as a good example for whoever hopes in God and the last day.

studies.applyIt: Think of a time someone did not explain something to you but simply took you somewhere: a workshop, a hospital, a meeting they knew you needed to see. That is the verb this ayah uses. Do that for someone this week. Take them along rather than telling them about it, and let the place do the explaining.

studies.title: Seven Heavens And Their Like
studies.meaning: The surah's last ayah moves as far from its subject as it is possible to go, and then comes back. Seven heavens are named and then something of the earth like them, a phrase the commentators discuss at length without settling: some read it as seven earths, others as a likeness in structure rather than in number, and the range is preserved. The command is described as descending between them continuously. Then the purpose clause, which is the point: so that you may know two things, that God is capable and that His knowledge encompasses everything.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The commentators note the return the ayah makes: a chapter that began with a woman's position in a house ends with the structure of the cosmos, and the purpose clause connects them, since what is at stake in the household passage is whether God knows and can act. No occasion is reported. Classical readers treat the ayah as the surah's answer to everything the earlier instructions had asked people to trust.

keyTerms.note: A word for a counterpart or a parallel, not necessarily a duplicate. Its openness is why the commentators offer several readings of what exactly is being compared, and they record the range rather than choosing one.
An intensive form implying descent by stages and repeatedly, rather than a single arrival. The tense is present, so what is described is continuous traffic rather than an event that finished.

A verb for enclosing something on every side, used of a wall around a garden. Applied to knowledge it says nothing lies outside rather than that everything is known, which is a picture instead of a list.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Seven was the number for completeness in that world rather than an inventory. Seven nights, seven circuits, seven sleepers, seven ears of grain: the count marked a whole rather than a total, in the same way a modern speaker says a dozen without counting. Arabians navigating by stars had a working picture of layered skies from the traditions around them, and the ayah speaks into that picture rather than correcting it.
studies.didYouKnow: This is the only place in the Quran where the earth is described as having a like of the seven heavens, and the phrasing is deliberately compressed: it says of the earth their like, without a verb. Classical commentators list several readings and decline to choose, which is unusual for a statement about the structure of creation.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah gives a reason for cosmology, which is rare. The heavens are not described for their own sake but so that you may know, and the two things to be known are power and knowledge, exactly the two a person needs when their situation is beyond their control. Placed at the end of a surah about a marriage coming apart, the scale is not a change of subject. It is the ground under everything the chapter has asked for.

crossReferences.why: Describes seven heavens in layers and invites the reader to look for any flaw in them.
States that God fashioned the heavens into seven, and is knowing of all things.
Shows the angels and the spirit descending by permission with every command, on a single night.

studies.applyIt: Next time something in your life is genuinely outside your control, say the two claims in this ayah out loud: that God is able, and that nothing is outside His knowledge. Say them as statements, not as comfort. The surah puts them last, after eleven ayat of practical instruction, which suggests they are meant to be reached rather than started from.
